title: Racks that move together
prompt:
Last Tuesday, the rack whose breaker tripped had a distinctive daily power profile. Find the racks whose profiles have the same *shape*, whatever their size.

Write `most_similar(q, P, k)`. `q` has shape (24,), one value per hour; `P` has shape (n, 24), one rack per row. Return the indices of the `k` rows of `P` most similar to `q` by **centered cosine similarity** (subtract each profile's own mean, then take the cosine), most similar first.

A rack with a perfectly flat profile has no shape, so its similarity is undefined: never return it. If fewer than `k` racks qualify, return all of them. No Python loops.
hints: Two racks with the same shape but different sizes should score 1. Which part of each profile carries its size, and which part its shape?

Subtract each row's mean (keepdims=True), and the query's mean. The cosine of the centered vectors is the dot product divided by both norms. A flat row centers to all zeros, so its norm is 0: mark it as −inf (or drop it) before sorting rather than dividing by zero.

Pc = P - P.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True); qc = q - q.mean(); norms = np.linalg.norm(Pc, axis=1); sims = np.full(len(P), -np.inf); ok = norms > 0; sims[ok] = (Pc[ok] @ qc) / (norms[ok] * np.linalg.norm(qc)); order = np.argsort(-sims, kind="stable"); keep only entries of order whose similarity is finite, then the first k.

misconceptions.cosine-needs-centering: Raw cosine similarity on positive data is dominated by the shared baseline: two profiles with opposite daily shapes can score above 0.9. Center first; the cosine of centered vectors is the Pearson correlation.
misconceptions.cosine-zero-vector: A zero vector has no direction, so its cosine with anything is undefined (0/0 = NaN). Exclude it explicitly.
